profiles.name: Wilmer Estrada
profiles.description: One of approximately 1,500 activists arrested between 1999 and 2003 for civil disobedience at the U.S. Navy's Atlantic Fleet Weapons Training Facility on the island of Vieques, Puerto Rico. The campaign — sparked by the April 19, 1999 death of civilian Navy security guard David Sanes Rodríguez when an errant Marine F/A-18 bomb struck his observation post — drew Puerto Ricans of every political stripe (independentistas, statehooders, the Catholic Church, fishers, environmentalists) into a sustained nonviolent direct-action campaign demanding the Navy leave Vieques. Defendants were prosecuted in U.S. District Court for the District of Puerto Rico under 18 U.S.C. § 1382 (entering a military reservation) and typically served 30 to 90 days in federal custody, most often at MDC Guaynabo. The Navy formally ceased operations on Vieques on May 1, 2003. Listed as a current prisoner in Nuclear Resister Issue #121 "Inside & Out" prisoner roster.
profiles.finding: Colombian boxing presenter Wilmer Estrada Ponce and Nicaraguan developer are unlinked namesakes. Puerto Rico legislator Wilmer Estrada Cruz and Tito Kayak case witness are unverified identity leads; no portrait accepted.

profiles.name: Ali Rehman
profiles.description: Ali Rehman, also identified in the indictment as Faisal Ali Rehman, was a resident of Pakistan charged by a federal grand jury in Miami on May 12, 2011 with conspiring to support the Pakistani Taliban. The indictment alleged that he helped provide guns and money. Unlike the defendants arrested in South Florida, Rehman remained in Pakistan. No available federal record documents his arrest, extradition, U.S. booking or confinement.
profiles.finding: Actor Ali Rehman Khan, Swat commander killed in 2008 and Ali Rehman alias Taha Swati are not independently matched to Faisal Ali Rehman in the Miami indictment.

profiles.name: George Sexton
profiles.description: George Sexton is a conservation organizer and longtime conservation director of the Klamath-Siskiyou Wildlands Center. He was arrested while protesting exclusion of the public from a forestry-industry meeting at Southern Oregon University in 2004. He was also identified with defendants challenging Oregon’s Interfering with Agricultural Operations law after arrests connected to protests against Biscuit timber-sale logging. The Oregon Supreme Court held the law unconstitutional in 2009. Available accounts do not establish Sexton’s exact arrest day, booking interval or individual sentence.
profiles.finding: Official KS Wild staff page establishes identity, but downloaded 2500x1596 photograph shows subject from behind with face obscured; rejected as an unsuitable recognizable portrait.

profiles.name: Khalid Al-Sudanee
profiles.description: Khalid Al-Sudanee was the Jordan-based regional director of the Middle East office of the Islamic African Relief Agency. A federal grand jury in Missouri indicted him in March 2007 with the U.S. branch of the charity and several associates, alleging sanctions, money-laundering and conspiracy offenses involving transfers to Iraq. The indictment identifies him as a Jordanian resident born in 1951. Unlike several U.S.-based codefendants, available court records do not document that Al-Sudanee was arrested, extradited, tried or confined in the United States.

profiles.finding: Govinfo court record and DOJ indictment corroborate IARA identity. No verified portrait located; no other defendant's image substituted.

profiles.name: Kyle Snyder
profiles.description:
Kyle Snyder, born September 12, 1983 and raised partly in foster care in Colorado, enlisted in the United States Army in 2004 and served in Iraq with the 94th Engineers out of Fort Leonard Wood. In 2005, while on mid-tour leave, he went to Canada, called the war illegal and immoral, and applied for refugee status. On October 31, 2006 he held a press conference and then surrendered to Army authorities at Fort Knox, Kentucky, having been told through his lawyer that he would be discharged quickly and not imprisoned; when he was instead faced with returning to Iraq or going to prison, he left again and travelled the United States speaking against the war.

On February 23, 2007 he was arrested by police in Nelson, British Columbia, at the request of the United States Army. The police had no warrant; he was taken in wearing a robe and boxer shorts, not permitted to dress or to call his lawyer, and was released after roughly six hours when immigration officials confirmed there was no legal basis to hold him.

Whereabouts unverified: no credible recent source has been found locating him, and his country is uncertain — Canada or unknown. No exile start date is recorded on his case, because his time abroad was interrupted by the October 2006 surrender and nothing has documented his location since February 2007. He is recorded here as currently in exile on the assumption that he remains abroad.
profiles.finding: Wikipedia military portrait is only 86x121 pixels: reject as too small. Fire This Time 2005 rally photograph remains a source to inspect. Olympic wrestler namesake rejected.

profiles.name: Robert S. Zabala
profiles.description: Robert S. Zabala was a U.S. Marine reservist who sought discharge as a conscientious objector during the Iraq War era. After the military denied his application, he petitioned the federal court for relief. On March 29, 2007, U.S. District Judge James Ware granted habeas relief and ordered the Marine Corps to discharge him with Class 1-O conscientious-objector status within fifteen days. The court found no evidence that his application was merely an attempt to avoid an imminent Iraq deployment. This was a civil challenge to military service, not a criminal conviction or prison sentence.
profiles.finding: Govinfo conscientious-objector case and Courage to Resist profile index identify Robert Zabala. Index photo is a lead; host returned 403 for another profile during this run, so direct asset verification remains pending. Obituary of 63-year-old Robert Zabala not matched.

profiles.name: Brandon Hughey
profiles.description: Brandon Hughey was a U.S. Army private who went to Canada in 2004 rather than deploy to Iraq. He sought refugee protection and publicly opposed the war. This profile records his historical resistance and refuge claim; it does not establish a criminal conviction, prison term, or present immigration status.
profiles.finding: Fire This Time interview and Island Tides report establish war-resister identity and remain photo leads. Alabama attorney Brandon Hughey portraits rejected as unlinked namesake.

profiles.name: Corey Glass
profiles.description: Corey Glass, also documented as James Corey Glass, served in the U.S. Army National Guard and went to Canada in 2006 rather than return to Iraq. Amnesty International highlighted his conscientious objection and opposed his threatened deportation. Canada's Federal Court stayed his removal on July 9, 2008. The potential military prosecution described by his supporters was a risk, not an established conviction or prison sentence. His present immigration status is not established here.
profiles.finding: Real News interview and ABC report establish war-resister identity. Indybay protest photographs do not by themselves establish that Glass is pictured; no portrait accepted yet.

profiles.name: Darrell Anderson
profiles.description: Darrell Anderson was a U.S. Army specialist who served in Baghdad in 2004 and went to Canada rather than return to Iraq. He publicly opposed the war and returned to U.S. military control in October 2006. He was held for three days, released, and received an other-than-honorable discharge. That brief detention was not a court-martial prison sentence.
profiles.finding: Courage to Resist source returned 403; Frank Kuin page presented request-verification screen. Evergreen-hosted report credits a portrait to Elliot Stoller and remains a lead for extraction/quality review. No image deployed.

profiles.name: Mary Hanna
profiles.description: Mary Hanna was a U.S. Army captain, physician and anesthesiologist who entered the Army Health Professions Scholarship Program in 1997. She applied for conscientious-objector discharge in December 2005 after concluding that participation in war conflicted with her Christian faith. A federal district court granted habeas relief on October 6, 2006, and the First Circuit affirmed on January 18, 2008. The case ended her military obligation and did not involve arrest, criminal prosecution or confinement.
profiles.finding: First Circuit opinion establishes Army physician conscientious-objector identity; no verified portrait located.
